title: Death by a Thousand Caveats
author: The Disruptive Educator
summary: Writing as a self-described advocate for explicit instruction, the author names and diagnoses a specific rhetorical move in education debates: 'death by a thousand caveats,' the practice of picking apart individual studies' contextual limitations until no evidence is left standing. The piece argues that demanding a study be conducted in one's own exact classroom before accepting its relevance sets an impossible bar that no research could ever clear, and that context is better understood as something professional judgment applies evidence to, not a reason to dismiss evidence altogether. Drawing an analogy to medicine, the author contends that individual variation among students no more invalidates a broad evidence base than it invalidates the practice of prescribing medication based on population-level trial data. The essay leans on an AERO review of 328 studies supporting explicit instruction's effectiveness across contexts and Australia's NAPLAN underperformance data to argue that relying on professional judgment alone, absent evidence, has not closed achievement gaps. It closes by redefining professional judgment not as license to reject evidence but as the skill of translating a probabilistic, population-level finding into a specific classroom's circumstances.
points: The essay names a specific evasive tactic in evidence debates -- 'death by a thousand caveats' -- where legitimate points about context are stacked until they function to dismiss an entire evidence base rather than to refine its application.
The demand that a study match 'this teacher, these students, this school' before it counts is an unreachable standard that, if applied consistently, would leave no research usable by anyone.

The medicine analogy reframes context: doctors don't discard population-level drug trial data because two patients respond differently; they use professional judgment to apply generalizable evidence to the individual case in front of them.

AERO's review of more than 328 studies is invoked as exactly the kind of replication-across-populations evidence base that should settle whether explicit instruction 'works' in general, even though no single study was conducted in any specific reader's classroom.
quotes: There's nothing wrong with identifying limitations in research. The problem is when this becomes death by a thousand caveats: finding enough reasons that individual pieces of evidence don't apply until we're left with no evidence at all.

However, if we require the evidence to have been generated in circumstances nearly identical to ours before we're willing to engage with it, then we very quickly arrive at a standard that almost no evidence will meet.

Underneath all of this is something important: the existence of individual variation doesn't render the broader body of evidence useless. Nor does the existence of evidence remove the need for professional judgment. A decision is informed by the evidence, interpreted through professional expertise and adapted to the context in which it is being applied.

To understand whether explicit instruction is effective across different contexts, AERO conducted a review of more than 328 studies. The review found that explicit instruction is an effective teaching practice across a variety of contexts and for different subgroups of students.
Professional judgment isn't the thing that decides whether the evidence applies; it's the thing that helps you translate evidence into a particular classroom context.
So, no, that study probably wasn't done in your classroom. But, like most research, that doesn't mean it has nothing to tell you about what happens there.
